walkthroughs.body_html:
Real reactions rarely make as much product as the equation predicts.

Why not? Losses in filtering, side reactions, or the reaction doesn't fully complete.

% yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100

Worked example: predicted 40 g, got 30 g. % yield = 30 ÷ 40 × 100 = 75%.

Atom economy asks: how much of the reactant mass ends up as useful product?

% atom economy = (Mr of useful products ÷ total Mr of reactants) × 100

Worked example: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. If CO₂ is the useful product: Mr useful = 44, total reactants = 16 + 64 = 80. Atom economy = 44 ÷ 80 × 100 = 55%.

Yield tells you how much you actually get. Atom economy tells you how much is wasted as by-products.

Sustainable reactions need both high yield AND high atom economy.

That's why industries choose reaction pathways carefully — fewer waste atoms means cheaper and greener.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct formula for percentage yield?
options: (theoretical ÷ actual) × 100
(actual ÷ theoretical) × 100
actual − theoretical
(actual × theoretical) ÷ 100

mcqs.q: Why is atom economy important in industry?
options: It speeds up reactions
It reduces waste and is more sustainable
It increases boiling point
It removes the need for a catalyst

mcqs.q: What does a mole of a substance represent?
options: A mole is a unit of mass equal to the relative molecular mass in grams of any substance.
Avogadro's number (6.02 x 10^23) of particles of that substance.
Different gases occupy completely different volumes proportional to their molar mass.
A mole is a unit of volume equal to 24 dm^3 at any temperature.

mcqs.q: At room temperature and pressure, what volume does 1 mole of any gas occupy?
options: The new concentration is 2 mol/dm^3 because adding water makes the solution stronger.
Different gases occupy completely different volumes proportional to their molar mass.
Approximately 24 dm^3 (24,000 cm^3), regardless of the identity of the gas.
Heavier gases occupy a smaller volume per mole because their particles are denser.

mcqs.q: If 50 cm^3 of a 1 mol/dm^3 solution is diluted to 100 cm^3, what is the new concentration?
options: The new concentration is 2 mol/dm^3 because adding water makes the solution stronger.
The new concentration is 0.05 mol/dm^3 because you doubled the volume so you halve the concentration once and shift the decimal too.
0.5 mol/dm^3 — the moles stay the same but the volume doubled.
A mole is a unit of volume equal to 24 dm^3 at any temperature.
